routes.description: Establish that evolved religious stories, God-language, and biblical tradition encode indispensable interpretive structures through which moral facts acquire normative force, recurrent patterns become intelligible, and truthful conduct becomes practically embodied.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by showing that bare facts and explicit rational instruction are insufficient for grounding and transmitting value, while a developmental and psychologically informed reading of religious tradition can preserve truth-seeking, moral universals, and effective guidance without requiring rigid literalism.

motionBridge.description: Show that religious narrative supplies a necessary or materially superior interpretive framework connecting reality to moral value, meaning, and conduct.

centralBridges.description: Explain why facts require antecedent moral intuitions or narrative structures before they can yield judgments about better and worse states.
Establish a constrained developmental method by which biblical stories and God-language express recurring psychological, social, and moral realities.
Show that deeper cross-context patterns can survive cultural variation and orient objective moral judgment without collapsing into relativism.
Explain how personified stories, inherited practices, conscience, sacrifice, and truthful speech embody moral guidance more effectively than abstract propositions alone.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the general human danger of fundamentalism from religion itself and show how religious tradition can subordinate fixed dogma to truthful inquiry.
Connect evolved interpretive structures and cultural inheritance to the formation and transmission of durable moral intuitions.

routes.description: Establish that objective concern for conscious well-being, reality-directed inquiry, and revisable causal understanding can ground moral truth and meaning without biblical authority, while dogma, immoral texts, unconstrained reinterpretation, and ambiguous God-language weaken the religious alternative.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by providing a coherent nonreligious basis for objective value and meaningful life, then showing that open inquiry can retain useful psychological or cultural insights while correcting harmful, obsolete, or unsupported religious commitments.

motionBridge.description: Show that facts about conscious experience and honest inquiry adequately ground moral truth and meaning, making dogmatic religious frameworks unnecessary and comparatively unreliable.

centralBridges.description: Ground objective moral distinctions in the intrinsic badness of universal misery and the full range of consequences for conscious beings.
Establish reality-directed, evidence-sensitive inquiry as the common basis for knowledge and the correction of moral rules as causal understanding improves.
Show how explicit immoral commands and revelation claims obstruct correction and give literal fundamentalism continuing persuasive resources.
Demonstrate that literal readings preserve harmful commitments while increasingly metaphorical readings depend on standards external to scripture.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for spiritual, introspective, and morally transformative experiences through universal facts about consciousness and human psychology.
Test religious authority through conflicting traditions and assess whether unconventional God-language misleadingly validates ordinary supernatural beliefs.

sections.title: Moral Facts, Well-Being, and the Fact–Value Bridge
sections.rationale: This issue contains the foundational clash over whether conscious suffering and flourishing can terminate moral reasoning or whether facts become normative only through antecedent intuitions and narrative interpretation.

sections.title: Scriptural Authority and Interpretive Constraint
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether developmental and psychological readings can extract defensible biblical truth while remaining textually constrained, especially when confronting explicit immoral or apocalyptic material.

sections.title: God-Language, Prayer, and Naturalized Spirituality
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether pragmatic accounts of God and prayer identify realities best expressed through religious language or merely redescribe psychological and social processes available to secular explanation.

sections.title: Moral Universals, Cultural Variation, and Religious Pluralism
sections.rationale: This issue assesses whether recurrent structures across stories, cultures, and disciplines constrain moral interpretation or whether incompatible traditions undermine claims of distinctive religious authority.

sections.title: Dogmatism, Truthful Speech, and Revisable Inquiry
sections.rationale: This issue compares the claim that religious symbolism can elevate truthful correction above fixed dogma with the secular claim that evidence-sensitive inquiry is a clearer and more reliable safeguard against error.

sections.title: Inherited Heuristics and Practical Moral Guidance
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether culturally embodied stories guide conduct where rational instruction is behaviorally weak or instead preserve mistaken rules that causal knowledge can revise and replace.

routes.description: Establish that theistic idealism provides a more plausible unified explanation than naturalism for consciousness, emergent physical reality, objective morality, and the ultimate cosmological foundation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if mind is shown to be irreducible and explanatorily fundamental, the disputed phenomena support a necessary personal ground, and one unlimited mind explains the total evidence with greater comparative economy than the naturalistic alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect the combined evidence from consciousness, emergence, morality, and cosmology to the conclusion that theism is more plausible than naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Show that conscious experience is not reducible to physical computation and that physical reality can coherently be understood as emergent from mind.
Show that the informational, relational, quantum, and structurally mind-like features of the universe support a mental rather than self-sufficient material foundation.
Show that contingent minds and objective personal moral obligations require a necessary and perfect personal ground.
Show that one unlimited mind explains the debated domains with fewer independent brute commitments than the naturalistic cosmological and reductive alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish that the proposed lawless or minimally specified natural origin lacks an adequate causal and probabilistic basis for producing the observed universe.
Defend the claim that an unlimited partless mind can be ontologically simple despite possessing maximal knowledge, power, and explanatory scope.

routes.description: Establish that secular naturalism is more plausible because physical and evolutionary mechanisms explain the disputed evidence, while a minimally specified natural origin is simpler and predicts the observed world better than a perfect divine mind.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the detailed evidence concerning brains, cosmic structure, moral development, and natural causal precedent is more expected under naturalism, and if theistic unification depends on unsupported reductions or a highly specified divine posit.

motionBridge.description: Connect naturalistic explanations and likelihood comparisons across all four evidential domains to the conclusion that theism is not more plausible than naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Show through computational modeling, neural intervention, comparative anatomy, and evolution that consciousness depends causally on physical brain systems.
Explain cosmic and neural structural similarities through ordinary physical organization rather than treating them as evidence of universe-scale mentality.
Ground moral imperatives without a divine person and show that gradual, error-prone moral development is expected under naturalism.
Show that a minimally specified random origin or sparse brute foundation is simpler than an omniscient, omnipotent, and morally perfect mind.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Apply parsimony, established causal precedent, and comparative evidential likelihood to the complete set of disputed phenomena.
Explain why privileged first-person access to an instantiated computation does not prevent third-person neural evidence from supporting physicalism.

sections.rationale: Whether subjective experience is irreducible or instead caused by computational brain systems determines the foundational contrast between idealism and physicalism and bears directly on which worldview predicts embodied consciousness.

sections.title: Emergence, Information, and Cosmic Structure
sections.rationale: The competing interpretations of fundamental physics, quantum cognition, and cosmic-neural resemblance determine whether emergent physical reality supplies positive evidence for a mind-like foundation or ordinary physical organization.

sections.title: Morality, Obligation, and Historical Development
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether objective obligations require a transcendent personal source or can arise as empirically grounded overriding imperatives, including which account better anticipates the observed development of moral practice.

sections.title: Cosmological Origins, Probability, and Brute Facts
sections.rationale: The coherence and generative adequacy of a lawless or minimally specified origin are central to whether naturalism offers a genuine cosmological alternative and whether its brute commitments are preferable to a necessary mind.

sections.title: Parsimony, Prediction, and Explanatory Unification
sections.rationale: The motion ultimately requires comparing the total explanatory scope, prior plausibility, predictive fit, and ontological commitments of one unlimited divine mind with the naturalistic accounts offered across all four evidential domains.

routes.description: Establish human flourishing as the shared comparative standard, then show that secular humanism better advances it through revisable evidence-based inquiry, contextual moral reasoning, and consequence-sensitive conflict resolution.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the secular framework supplies defensible methods for rational and moral decisions, connects those methods to human welfare, answers the foundational objections, and supports comparative superiority over Christian authority.

motionBridge.description: Connect secular humanism's goals, methods, and practical consequences to superior achievement of the motion's four stated domains.

centralBridges.description: Justify human flourishing and empirically informed human interests as a meaningful common standard for comparing the worldviews.
Show how revisability, logical testing, experience, and independent corroboration support rational decisions despite acknowledged fallibility.
Explain how objective, value-relative and context-sensitive assessment can guide conduct by its effects on human welfare.
Demonstrate how secular principles address cooperation, equality, peace, and doctrinal conflict more reliably than unsupported authority claims.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the position that using logic and reliable inquiry need not include an ultimate account of their origin or a guarantee of certainty.
Explain why comparative claims about flourishing should depend on evidenced human consequences rather than unverified supernatural rewards.

routes.description: Establish that comparative superiority requires a coherent objective foundation, then argue that Christianity grounds rational intelligibility, moral obligation, and human flourishing while secular humanism cannot justify its own standards.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if secular humanism's accounts of cognition, scientific inference, and welfare-based ethics are shown to be circular or self-undermining, while Christian foundations provide a coherent basis for reason, morality, and flourishing.

motionBridge.description: Connect Christianity's claimed foundations for intelligibility, ethics, and flourishing to superiority across the motion's comparative domains.

centralBridges.description: Require a worldview-neutral, non-question-begging standard capable of supporting a genuine judgment of comparative superiority.
Show why physically caused cognition and intersubjective checking require an account of reliable access to mind-independent logical truth.
Ground logic, scientific presuppositions, and nature's uniformity in God's rational character and the design of human minds.
Ground moral duties in divine character and revelation while explaining why chosen goals and consequences cannot justify themselves.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect biblical instructions concerning love of God and neighbor to a substantive Christian account of human flourishing.
Establish freedom from self-refutation as a threshold condition for trusting a worldview's conclusions about welfare and conduct.

sections.title: Comparative Standard and the Meaning of Flourishing
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether human welfare supplies a shared basis for comparison or whether superiority requires a further objective and worldview-neutral standard.

sections.title: Cognition, Logical Inference, and Epistemic Reliability
sections.rationale: The dispute over physical cognition, fallibility, correspondence, and independent corroboration bears directly on each worldview's capacity for rational decision-making.

sections.title: Foundations of Logic, Science, and Intelligibility
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether practical reliance on logic and science is sufficient or whether their presuppositions require a specifically Christian metaphysical foundation.

sections.title: Moral Standards, Consequences, and Context
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of objective revelation and welfare-based contextual judgment form the central clash over how moral claims are justified and applied.

sections.title: Practical Outcomes, Cooperation, and Conflict Resolution
sections.rationale: This issue connects the foundational disputes to equality, peace, scriptural disagreement, present-life welfare, and the practical resolution of human conflicts.

motionBridge.description: The historical evidence and relevant background information must make Jesus's resurrection the best explanation of the reported postmortem appearances.

centralBridges.description: Early and corroborated sources must establish individual, hostile, and group appearance claims as data requiring explanation.
Resurrection must provide greater explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and economy than hallucination or other naturalistic alternatives.
Historical inquiry must be able to recognize an event transcending known natural capacities without first identifying its precise supernatural agent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Independent allegedly paranormal phenomena may supply background plausibility for admitting supernatural explanations.
Reliable ordinary testimonial evidence must be capable in principle of supporting an extraordinary historical event.

routes.description: Maintain that resurrection proponents bear the evidential burden, challenge the accessibility and reliability of the ancient appearance reports, and deny that unexplained events or defeated natural alternatives establish supernatural causation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical data remain insufficiently confirmed or if resurrection and divine agency cannot be warranted from those data, making suspension of belief appropriate without requiring proof that resurrection was impossible.

motionBridge.description: Belief in Jesus's resurrection must be withheld unless the affirmative evidence establishes both the alleged event and the inferential move to resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Ancient appearance reports must provide accessible, independently supportable evidence adequate to establish the claimed postmortem events.
An unexplained or anomalous event must not be treated as evidence of supernatural causation without a method that distinguishes that cause from error, fraud, hallucination, or unknown natural causes.
The resurrection hypothesis must supply testable or discriminating explanatory content rather than merely relabeling the absence of a natural explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The evidential limits created by two millennia of investigative distance must constrain comparisons with directly observable modern anomalies.
Attributing resurrection to divine action requires independent grounds for a capable and willing agent or evidence that itself discriminates in favor of such an agent.

sections.title: Historical foundation for the appearance claims
sections.rationale: The existence, independence, accessibility, and reliability of the Pauline, apostolic, individual, and group appearance traditions determine what historical data the competing explanations must address.

sections.title: Resurrection versus naturalistic explanations
sections.rationale: The motion turns centrally on whether resurrection explains the asserted historical data better than hallucination, error, dishonesty, or other naturalistic possibilities under comparative explanatory criteria.

sections.title: From anomaly to supernatural causation
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether an event judged incompatible with known natural capacities may be classified as supernatural or whether that classification merely substitutes a label for unresolved causation.

sections.title: Historical method and standards for extraordinary claims
sections.rationale: The parties' competing standards for testimony, repeatability, methodological naturalism, and investigation determine what kinds of evidence can justify an extraordinary historical conclusion.

sections.title: Background supernaturalism and identification of divine agency
sections.rationale: Allegedly paranormal phenomena and the question of prior grounds for God affect the background plausibility of resurrection and the further inference from a postmortem event to purposeful divine action.

routes.description: Establish Christianity through a cumulative metaphysical route from unavoidable logic and contingent reality to a necessary self-relating Logos, then identify its universal, particular, and individual structure with the Trinity and defend the coherence of divine self-knowledge, creation, and hiddenness.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if indispensable logical and explanatory relations require a necessary mental ground, the proposed structure warrants a specifically Trinitarian identification rather than generic theism, and the account remains coherent under objections concerning divine perfection, revelation, creation, and hiddenness.

motionBridge.description: Connect the necessary self-relating Logos to distinctively Christian Trinitarian truth rather than stopping at logic, a first cause, idealism, or generic divinity.

centralBridges.description: Show that logic is unavoidable and describes the objective self-relating structure of reality requiring the proposed Logos account.
Show that contingent reality and rational explanation terminate in an uncaused necessary foundation rather than an infinite regress or brute physical fact.
Justify identifying the interdependence of universality, particularity, and individuality with a mental and specifically Trinitarian Logos.
Reconcile divine perfection and timeless knowledge with self-relation, doubt, creation, and contingent truths without introducing contradiction or dependence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how natural reason can disclose the relevant Trinitarian structure while accounting for Christianity's historical and incarnational claims.
Show why religious doubt, historical variation, divine transcendence, and creation from nothing remain compatible with the proposed God.

routes.description: Reject the motion by applying correspondence, demonstration, and explanatory economy to the Logos case, showing that its inferences do not establish a unique necessary mind or Christianity and that hiddenness and internal tensions provide contrary evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if logic and reality can be treated without adding God, the transitions from first cause or logical categories to a mind and Trinity remain unsupported, or the proposed Christian account conflicts with divine perfection, historical accessibility, classical logic, or expected evidence.

motionBridge.description: Connect the affirmative case's evidential, inferential, or coherence failures to withholding affirmation that Christianity is true and to any supported contrary inference.

centralBridges.description: Defend correspondence with demonstrable reality and minimal explanatory commitments as the appropriate standard for the Christian truth claim.
Show that a regress terminus, necessary foundation, logical structure, or mind does not establish a unique cause, Trinity, incarnation, or Catholic Christianity.
Show that an omniscient perfect mind cannot genuinely doubt, learn, deliberate, or correct itself in the manner required by the affirmative account.
Defend content-neutral classical logical laws against the dialectical unity of opposites used to support the affirmative metaphysics.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why divine hiddenness, unanswered prayer, religious competition, and historical variation count against the expected Christian world.
Distinguish conclusions arguably available through natural reason from historical claims about Jesus that require otherwise unavailable testimony or revelation.

sections.title: Truth Standards, Evidence, and Divine Hiddenness
sections.rationale: The motion requires a standard for affirming religious truth and an account of whether divine silence, disagreement, prayer, and historical variation fit or undermine Christianity.

sections.title: Grounding Logic and the Logos
sections.rationale: The central affirmative framework treats logic as unavoidable and as reality's objective self-relating structure, while the skeptical alternative disputes that God adds necessary grounding or explanation.

sections.title: Necessary Cause, Contingency, and Explanatory Termination
sections.rationale: The route from contingent reality to an uncaused foundation must establish an adequate terminus and address whether uniqueness, mentality, and explanatory resources follow from causal termination.

sections.title: From Metaphysical Structure to Trinity, Incarnation, and Revelation
sections.rationale: Christianity requires bridging generic metaphysical conclusions to the Trinity and historically specific claims about Jesus while resolving what natural reason can establish without revelation or testimony.

sections.title: Perfect Divine Knowledge, Doubt, and Self-Relation
sections.rationale: The extended dispute over whether perfect knowledge can include falsification, doubt, recursive correction, or foreknown resolution directly tests the coherence of the proposed Trinitarian mind and incarnation.

sections.title: Creation, Divine Relations, Spacetime, and Logical Coherence
sections.rationale: Claims about timeless creation, contingent truths, transcendence, spacetime, and unity of opposites test whether the proposed God can relate to creation without dependence, change, or conflict with classical logic.

routes.description: Establish that Christianity lacks proportionate rational warrant by applying consistent evidential standards to its supernatural claims and showing that revelation, doctrine, and theistic explanations do not overcome available objections or alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christianity's distinctive claims require support not supplied by transmitted testimony, religious experience, or worldview comparison, while unclear revelation, contested doctrine, and unresolved counterevidence prevent those claims from being rationally justified.

motionBridge.description: Connect inadequate support for Christianity's distinctive claims and material undefeated objections to the conclusion that Christianity is not rationally warranted.

centralBridges.description: Require evidence proportionate to supernatural claims and apply the same justificatory standard to Christianity and incompatible religions.
Show that indirect historical transmission, disputed revelation, and resurrection premises do not establish Christianity's conclusions about Jesus or God.
Provide non-theistic accounts of morality and fallible reasoning sufficient to resist claims that Christianity uniquely grounds value or rational inference.
Relate unclear communication, moral disagreement, and troubling scriptural claims to the expected attributes of an omnipotent and loving God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish atheism from materialism and determinism so that objections to those positions do not by themselves establish Christian rationality.
Explain how testing and verification can support rational inquiry despite uncertainty about evolved cognition.

routes.description: Establish that Christianity is rational through a cumulative comparative case in which theism accounts for cosmic order, objective value, and reason, while historical considerations and experience provide specifically Christian warrant.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christian belief can rest on good evidence without requiring certainty, Christianity supplies a coherent comparative explanation of reason and morality, and the resurrection and revelation claims remain historically and intellectually defensible against the principal objections.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative explanatory and historical case to the conclusion that accepting Christianity can be rational.

centralBridges.description: Show that fine-tuning and mathematical intelligibility are better explained by purposive mind than by unguided alternatives.
Show that Christian theism can ground truth-directed reason, human dignity, moral obligation, and responsibility more coherently than reductive naturalism.
Establish sufficiently reliable access to early Christian claims and defend resurrection as an explanation of the relevant historical facts.
Explain how interpretive method, divine purposes, and qualified evidential access can answer objections from difficult scripture, disagreement, and uneven revelation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Define rationality so that good-faith disagreement and lack of certainty do not automatically make Christian belief irrational.
Integrate personal experience and Christianity's account of meaning and hope as supporting considerations within the wider case.

sections.title: Evidential Standards, Revelation, and Access
sections.rationale: Determines what rational belief requires, whether one standard is applied across religions, and whether disagreement, personal experience, unequal access, and the chosen mode of revelation bear on Christian warrant.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Intelligibility, and Theistic Explanation
sections.rationale: Tests whether fine-tuning and mathematical order materially support purposive mind, including the force of probability qualifications and the challenge that religious interpretation follows external scientific correction.

sections.title: Morality, Human Dignity, and Scriptural Coherence
sections.rationale: Covers rival accounts of moral obligation and human value together with disagreement, justice and mercy, and difficult biblical narratives that test Christianity's claimed moral coherence.

sections.title: Reason, Freedom, Evolution, and Naturalism
sections.rationale: Addresses whether determined or evolved cognition can remain rationally trustworthy, whether theism supplies a better foundation for reason, and whether atheism is properly identified with the naturalistic positions under challenge.

sections.title: Resurrection, Testimony, and Christian-Specific Inference
sections.rationale: Examines the principal bridge from general theism to Christianity: the reliability of early testimony, the explanatory case for resurrection, and whether reported miracles entail the claimed identity and authority of Jesus.

routes.description: Establish that God-language legitimately identifies an experientially real and culturally indispensable religious substrate that organizes ultimate value, inherited moral knowledge, and action under existential uncertainty, rather than functioning as a dispensable supernatural hypothesis.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the functional, phenomenological, and metaphysical dimensions of God-language are sufficiently connected to show that reducing it to an unsupported claim about a bounded supernatural object misstates its referent and its indispensable orienting role.

motionBridge.description: Show that God-language names a form of reality expressed through transcendent experience, ultimate value, inherited wisdom, and existential orientation, even if that reality is not modeled as an ordinary material object.

centralBridges.description: Define God in terms broad enough to encompass the organizing hierarchy of ultimate value and inherited wisdom while remaining substantive enough to bear the motion.
Connect recurrent transcendent or mystical experience and its durable consequences to the religious concepts through which people interpret reality.
Explain why religious narrative and metaphor supply an embodied interpretive substrate for moral judgment, meaning, and conduct that explicit propositions or finite rules cannot replace.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show why consciousness and experienced reality complicate attempts to treat God solely as a bounded object within a consciousness-independent material model.
Identify the inherited or metaphysical value commitments presupposed by secular appeals to well-being, dignity, and moral restraint.

routes.description: Establish that the psychological, moral, and cultural usefulness of God-language neither demonstrates a supernatural agent nor makes religious framing indispensable, because naturalistic accounts can explain the relevant experiences, values, and social practices.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if metaphorical or pragmatic uses of God-language can be separated from claims about a supernatural being, those existence claims remain unjustified, and secular explanations adequately account for religious experience, morality, meaning, and inherited wisdom.

motionBridge.description: Show that God-language can perform important psychological, moral, or cultural functions without establishing that it refers to a real supernatural being.

centralBridges.description: Maintain the distinction between the usefulness of religious belief and the evidential warrant required for a supernatural existence claim.
Provide naturalistic explanations for transcendent experience and supernatural attribution that do not infer an external deity from phenomenological intensity.
Account for moral responsibility, cooperation, revision, and progress through human goals, evidence, empathy, and social or evolutionary processes without divine authority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish poetic identification of God with truth or highest value from the traditional claim of a supernatural thinking creator or sustainer.
Show that useful knowledge inherited through religion can be retained and evaluated through human judgment without preserving supernatural belief.

sections.title: God-Language, Definition, and Ontological Reference
sections.rationale: The motion centrally turns on whether functional, metaphorical, phenomenological, and supernatural uses of the word God identify one defensible referent or improperly combine distinct claims.

sections.title: Religious Experience and Naturalistic Explanation
sections.rationale: Transcendent and mystical experiences support the religious-substrate route only if their interpretation and consequences bear on reality in a way not fully explained by culture, cognition, or material causes.

sections.title: Moral Grounding and Secular Alternatives
sections.rationale: The claimed indispensability of the religious substrate depends substantially on whether secular accounts can ground responsibility, well-being, cooperation, error correction, and moral progress without God-belief.

sections.title: Narrative Inheritance and Existential Orientation
sections.rationale: The debate requires assessing whether religious narrative uniquely preserves embodied wisdom and orientation amid uncertainty or whether its useful contents and functions remain available without supernatural commitment.

sections.title: Consciousness, Reality, and Explanatory Limits
sections.rationale: Disagreement about consciousness-independent reality and unresolved explanatory mysteries affects whether nonmaterial or metaphysical possibilities merit consideration, while also testing whether uncertainty can warrant a religious conclusion.

routes.description: Establish a historical core of Jesus' death, burial or empty tomb, and postmortem appearances, then show that bodily resurrection explains that core within an adequately supported theistic framework.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical premises are sufficiently supported, bodily resurrection accounts for them more adequately than the live natural alternatives, and objections concerning testimony, prior probability, and miracle attribution do not defeat the inference.

motionBridge.description: Connect the supported historical core and comparative explanation directly to the rational conclusion that Jesus bodily rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Establish Jesus' death and burial or empty tomb together with reported postmortem experiences sufficiently robust to require explanation.
Show that the appearance and resurrection traditions concern a transformed physical body rather than only an inward or immaterial experience.
Show that hallucination, removal, survival, fraud, legend, and combinations of such accounts do not explain the historical core as adequately.
Provide sufficient background warrant for divine action and connect that framework specifically to Jesus so resurrection is an admissible historical explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the early, eyewitness-linked, and mutually reinforcing character of the traditions used to establish the historical premises.
Use claimed anomalous or survival evidence to challenge strict naturalistic exclusion without treating that evidence itself as proof of resurrection.

routes.description: Show that the partisan and limited historical record does not distinguish bodily resurrection from visionary, removal, error-based, or presently unreconstructable alternatives under an appropriate standard for miracle attribution.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if indispensable historical or bodily premises remain uncertain, the evidence remains underdetermined by available alternatives, or justified background beliefs about supernatural agency are insufficient to make resurrection the warranted conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Connect unresolved historical and epistemic underdetermination directly to the conclusion that bodily resurrection is not established by the evidence.

centralBridges.description: Show that chronology, partisan sourcing, limited independent testimony, and textual ambiguity constrain the historical premises available for the resurrection inference.
Show that grief visions, hallucination, body removal, error, or combinations of ordinary possibilities can resist the resurrection inference without a complete reconstruction.
Challenge whether reported seeing, touching, and spiritual-body language establish an externally observable and coherent bodily resurrection.
Require independently justified beliefs about a supernatural agent, its nature, and its intentions before unexplained evidence may rationally be attributed to miracle.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Treat inability to reconstruct a distant event as a reason for a tentative conclusion rather than as affirmative support for resurrection.
Require appropriate repeatability or independent validation before anomalous perception reports alter the background case for supernatural survival.

sections.title: Historical Sources and Early Tradition
sections.rationale: The dating, provenance, independence, and eyewitness linkage of Pauline, creedal, Gospel, and non-Christian material determine the evidential foundation available to both burden routes.

sections.title: Death, Burial, and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: Actual death and the disposition of Jesus' body are indispensable to bodily resurrection, while the empty-tomb evidence and ordinary removal possibilities shape what requires explanation.

sections.title: Appearances and Psychological Alternatives
sections.rationale: The reported experiences of disciples, groups, Paul, and other converts form the principal experiential basis of the case and the principal ground for visionary or hallucination accounts.

sections.title: Nature of the Resurrection Body
sections.rationale: Contact narratives, sensory reports, eating accounts, and Pauline spiritual-body language bear directly on whether the traditions support bodily resurrection rather than an immaterial manifestation.

sections.title: Comparative Explanation and Burden of Reconstruction
sections.rationale: The motion turns partly on whether resurrection must outperform a complete natural reconstruction or whether unresolved ordinary possibilities are enough to leave the evidence underdetermined.

sections.title: Miracle Priors and Worldview Evidence
sections.rationale: Prior beliefs about God, divine intention, natural law, anomalous perception, and survival after death affect when historical evidence can rationally support a specifically miraculous conclusion.

routes.description: Establish that the earliest Christian sources report Jesus as raised in bodily continuity, then support the historical credibility of those reports through transmission, attestation, and relevant circumstantial considerations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources can be treated as sufficiently early and historically connected to witnesses, their resurrection language is bodily rather than merely immaterial, and the principal skeptical alternatives do not defeat the resulting inference.

motionBridge.description: Connect credible early-source testimony to the historical conclusion that Jesus rose bodily from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Establish an early and multiply attested proclamation of burial, resurrection, and appearances.
Show that spiritual-body and related source language denotes transformed bodily continuity rather than a nonphysical survival claim.
Ground the relevant texts and early church testimony in a historically credible chain connected to apostolic witnesses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the claimed event from proposed pagan dying-and-rising parallels in chronology, content, and documentary support.
Explain how conversion, persecution, martyrdom traditions, and early expansion bear on the sincerity and claimed witness basis of the proclamation.

routes.description: Withhold the historical conclusion of bodily resurrection by applying inductive historical standards, challenging the sources' provenance and bodily meaning, and supplying analogues or ordinary explanations for the cited evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative evidence does not overcome the event's weak experiential analogy, the sources remain materially uncertain or internally disputed, or the supporting phenomena are adequately compatible with non-resurrection explanations.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available early Christian claims do not warrant concluding historically that Jesus bodily rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Require inductive and revisable historical inference while distinguishing divine possibility from evidence that this event occurred.
Challenge the provenance, coherence, and physical interpretation of the New Testament and patristic source base.
Place resurrection claims alongside ancient religious analogues and ordinary mechanisms capable of explaining belief formation and transmission.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether apostolic succession, named witnesses, and martyrdom traditions are independently verifiable rather than dependent on later institutional claims.
Separate sincere costly commitment and movement growth from the factual correctness of the resurrection proclamation.

sections.title: Historical Method, Miracle Possibility, and Evidential Burden
sections.rationale: This issue determines what kind of inference ancient testimony can support, how present experience and historical analogy constrain that inference, and why divine capability alone does or does not establish the reported event.

sections.title: Earliest Resurrection Sources and the Meaning of Bodily
sections.rationale: The motion turns directly on whether Paul and other early Christian texts proclaim bodily continuity, a transformed physical body, or a spiritual event that conflicts with later flesh-and-bones presentations.

sections.title: Source Provenance, Apostolic Transmission, and Multiple Attestation
sections.rationale: The historical force of the resurrection reports depends on authorship, authenticity, chronology, witness connection, cross-community transmission, and whether apparent convergence supplies independent attestation.

sections.title: Pagan Resurrection Parallels and Comparative Context
sections.rationale: Proposed Attis, Osiris, Baal, and related parallels bear on the use of historical analogy, the claimed uniqueness of the Christian account, and competing explanations of the narrative's religious context.

sections.title: Martyrdom, Conversion, and Early Christian Growth
sections.rationale: Costly commitment, apostolic martyrdom traditions, Paul's conversion, and movement expansion may support witness-based sincerity, while alternative social explanations test whether those facts establish more than belief.

routes.description: Establish that experienced evil and categorical moral obligation presuppose objective standards of goodness, then argue that those standards and the rational norms used to recognize them require a transcendent divine ground.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if objective moral obligations are warranted as more than evolved preferences, God provides their necessary ontological ground, and the proposed naturalistic explanations fail to account for moral and rational normativity without undermining themselves.

motionBridge.description: Connect the reality of evil through objective goodness and obligation to a divine ground adequate to explain them.

centralBridges.description: Establish that immediate moral experience warrants belief in categorical obligations that do not depend on individual or cultural attitudes.
Show that objective goodness and obligation require an ultimate standard grounded in God's nature rather than human preference.
Show that an unguided evolutionary account cannot both explain all beliefs causally and justify confidence in moral and rational beliefs as truth-directed.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Limit the moral argument to a divine moral ground while leaving identification of a particular religion to a cumulative case.
Distinguish disagreement or uncertainty about moral facts from evidence that no objective moral facts exist.

routes.description: Explain moral experience through evolved conscious psychology and shared practical aims while denying that its force, consensus, or emotional immediacy entails mind-independent value or a divine moral ground.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if agnostic atheism bears no unnecessary positive worldview burden, evolutionary and psychological processes adequately explain moral experience, and the pro case does not establish objective morality or derive God without circular or unsupported grounding assumptions.

motionBridge.description: Account for compelling moral experience without inferring mind-independent moral facts or accepting a divine moral ground.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish the psychological force of moral judgments from mind-independent truth and locate moral valuation in conscious attitudes.
Explain shared survival-oriented dispositions, practical moral rules, and disputed cases through evolutionary concern for flourishing and harm.
Show that explaining why moral judgments occur neither establishes their objective truth nor permits a divine mind to be assumed as their ground.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify agnostic atheism as nonbelief while identifying which additional naturalistic claims, if asserted, independently require support.
Treat reason as a necessary shared starting point for inquiry while distinguishing objective logical rules from conclusions dependent on adopted premises.

sections.title: Burden of Proof and Scope of the Moral Argument
sections.rationale: This issue fixes what agnostic atheism commits its defender to establish and whether the moral argument aims only at a divine moral ground or at a more specific religious conclusion.

sections.title: Objective Moral Obligation and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: This is the principal ontological clash: whether evil and categorical obligation disclose a mind-independent standard of goodness and whether such a standard requires grounding in God.

sections.title: Evolutionary and Psychological Explanation of Moral Experience
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether evolved dispositions, consciousness, flourishing, and harm can explain the felt force and broad convergence of morality without converting causal explanation into objective justification.

sections.title: Reason, Logic, and Evolutionary Reliability
sections.rationale: The competing accounts must address whether naturalistic evolution permits warranted trust in cognition and whether objective logical norms require a transcendent explanation or can function as shared assumptions.

sections.title: Moral Disagreement, Cultural Variation, and Practical Judgment
sections.rationale: Disagreement and ambiguous cases bear on whether moral experience is evidence of objective reality, cultural contingency, or merely limited access to truths that remain independent of judgment.
